_doc: CROSS-LANGUAGE reflect contract. The ts kernel (tests/reflect.test.ts) and the python kernel must BOTH reproduce every case's `expect` from `tree`+`bundles`. Edit here once; both runtimes re-verify. This is what keeps a second kernel from drifting. NOTE: the root reflect carries a per-runtime `runtime` field ("python"|"rust"|"swift"|"ts"); this fixture is exercised by the ts kernel so the root cases expect "ts". The root also carries deployment context `env` + `version` (read from FANTASTIC_ENV / FANTASTIC_VERSION on the host runtimes; the browser ts kernel has no env, so it is always env="host", version=null). Every reflect also carries `kernel_verbs` (#26): advertised on EVERY agent, answered by the root only. The ts kernel advertises the verbs IT answers (ps/cancel/ledger/ack_deadletter/kernel_start/shutdown_agents/kernel_stop) — python/rust/swift additionally list the tree-CRUD verbs they own, because this kernel genuinely has none: its tree is built by its bundles and persisted through the host loader, and advertising a verb it cannot answer would be a lie the model pays for. Every agent also carries the structural authority baseline {$self,$parent,$children} on BOTH `can_call` and `callable_by`, stamped and merged in the Agent constructor and surfaced by reflect (#7) — readable authority, so an agent is not left discovering its own reach by trial.

expect.sentence: Fantastic kernel. Everything is reachable by sending messages to agents.

kernel_verbs._: Kernel-owned: send to 'kernel'. The id you name is the OPERAND, not the actor. (`verbs` is what this agent itself does.) This kernel answers the verbs below; tree CRUD lives on the HOST root, reached over the bridge.
kernel_verbs.ps: args: limit:int?, after:int? — lists the LIVE dispatches (id, agent, verb), paged; an id is the message id of the call that started it.
kernel_verbs.cancel: args: task_id:int|str — kills that task AND ITS SUBTREE (a name kills the execution it names); returns {cancelled, killed:[ids]}; the blocked caller's item settles status:'cancelled'. An unknown or finished id kills nothing and says so.
kernel_verbs.ledger: args: limit:int?, after:int? — every execution YOU originated and what it became (id, target, status, attempts, retries, named, name?, outcome?, acked?), read from the kernel's memory store plus what is not yet flushed. `outcome` keeps the RESULT only for a named call; a dead letter keeps its error; anything else is {status, bytes}. Failed/timed_out/cancelled rows are the dead-letter queue (announced by the `on_deadletter` event): inspect, retry with a NEW id if you choose, then `ack_deadletter` it.
kernel_verbs.ack_deadletter: args: id:int|str (req — an execution id, or its name). Acknowledges a DEAD LETTER you originated — recorded in the kernel's store, it may then be pruned. Returns {acked:true, id}.
kernel_verbs.kernel_start: No args. THE START SEQUENCE — the root must name `memory_store_id` (fail loud otherwise): boots the root (it mints the guid), then that store, starts flushing the kernel's execution rows into it, then boots every other agent in registration order. Idempotent. Returns {started, store, booted:[ids]}.
kernel_verbs.shutdown_agents: No args. Stops the AGENTS, not the kernel: drains (new roots refused), sends `shutdown` to every agent advertising it, waits for in-flight work, cancels the rest. Returns {drained, shut:[ids], cancelled:[ids]}.
kernel_verbs.kernel_stop: No args. Stops this kernel gracefully — drain, every call settles (done, or cancelled into the dead letters), the last rows flush, the flusher stops. A browser kernel has no process to exit: it refuses new work until the page reloads.
